slides.0.title: Industry and Market
slides.0.subtitle: Wine Growers Canada, domestic share, exports, interprovincial shipping and US-alcohol bans
slides.1.title: Industry bodies and scale
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Wine Growers Canada
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Wine Growers Canada (founded 1967) represents roughly 90% of national production, with more than 800 winery establishments (canada.ca, 2022). Provinces have their own bodies, such as Wine Growers BC, Wine Country Ontario and Grape Growers of Ontario
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Economic-impact figures disagree
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Claims about total economic contribution vary by year and method: CAD 11.5 billion (2022 statement), about CAD 6.8 billion and 31,000 jobs (older), CAD 9.04 billion and 37,300 FTE jobs (2017 study via Fine Vintage) and CAD 10.1 billion GDP and about 100,000 jobs (WGC 2026). These are advocacy figures; the lesson only shows the need to cite year and source, and none is tested
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Domestic share
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Canadian wine is about 30% of domestic sales (WGC's 2026 paper says 29%); WGC and a Deloitte white paper propose a 51% target and a potential CAD 13.7 billion in value, an advocacy goal rather than the present state
slides.1.content: Always ask who said it and for which year.
slides.2.title: Exports and interprovincial trade
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Small exports
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Exports hit a record CAD 92 million in 2021, of which the US took CAD 73 million and China CAD 9 million (WGC advocacy material). Most wineries sell through their own cellar door and restaurants, with icewine dominating exports
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Interprovincial shipping
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Interprovincial alcohol shipping has long been restricted; in 2016 Manitoba, BC, Nova Scotia, Ontario and Quebec began allowing personal-use direct shipping, and in 2018 the Supreme Court rejected a bid for fully free trade (Fine Vintage). Provincial liquor boards and monopolies are a uniquely Canadian marketing structure
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Supermarket access
slides.2.highlights.2.content: BC opened supermarket wine sales in 2015 and Ontario in 2016, initially VQA wines only (Fine Vintage). VQA is about 11.3% of Ontario's volume and about 17.8% of BC's (Fine Vintage, 2019)
slides.2.content: Canada's wine market is cut up by provincial systems.
slides.3.title: Trade disputes and taxation
slides.3.highlights.0.title: 2025–26 US-alcohol bans
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Amid tariff disputes Ontario, Quebec and BC pulled US alcohol; Nova Scotia, PEI and Newfoundland sold off stock, while Alberta and Saskatchewan later restored US products. DISCUS says US liquor exports to Canada fell 63% in 2025 (single source); the 2026 CUSMA review remains uncertain
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Excise and domestic competition
slides.3.highlights.1.content: A WGC advocacy example says excise on 500,000 L is about CAD 372,500 in Canada against about CAD 27,000 for some foreign competitors (a single advocacy source, shown only to model the argument). Policies on domestic-grape producers have shifted repeatedly over time
slides.3.highlights.2.title: The end of Cellared in Canada
slides.3.highlights.2.content: From 12 March 2018 the CFIA banned the "Cellared in Canada" phrase; wines blended from imported bulk must state the countries of origin and no longer imply they are Canadian (Wikipedia). Outside VQA, other wording such as "Product of Canada" still has to be distinguished
slides.3.content: Market pressure comes from tariffs, tax and provincial systems.
